items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And he gave me permission after to do this.

ctx.x: Right, your stuff was in drawer back in the flood in New Orleans. So I would have to call up the social workers. At that point, we now had two more social workers that we hired instantly. One I hired on the street in my neighborhood, because she had just become a social worker and she was a mom in my kid’s class, and I adored her. I just said, “We need you” and she said yes. She’s been with us ten years, Alisa Hafkin. So if one person needs their apartment, now you have to call up the landlord of the place they…

give a month’s rent and a month’s security for everyone who needed it. But you don’t want to tell that to a landlord, because he’s going to figure after the first month he’s screwed. We know that they’ll be working, because we’re going to give them work in the Jazz in the Schools. But there’s a lot you don’t want to explain. So I would call up the potential landlord. They’d tell me they found a place, it looks great, “I told the landlord you’re my reference.” So I’d call up and that’s when I’d go into the British…
Would you do the British accent for us?

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: So we got Cos, he said he’d do it and it just started snowballing.

ctx.x: coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could…

was like this is incredible. “I’m going to give you my top producer.” And he gave us Rick White which was amazing, and Dan Melnick. And then some of the guys on our board, Bob Cranshaw and Jimmy Owens, they started reaching out to musicians. At the time I asked if anyone knew anyone famous. Someone had the number for Bill Cosby’s agent, so I left word. I remember a week later I get a call and I hear this guy with this voice that sounds familiar go, “Wendy?” I was like, “Yes.” He goes, “This is Cos.” Okay. This is…
